analysis.one_liner: Requires farm equipment makers to sell farmers the parts, tools, and manuals needed to fix their own machines.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with one cosponsor, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on February 1, 2022, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require farm equipment manufacturers to provide equipment owners and independent repair shops with the documentation, parts, software, and tools they need to diagnose, maintain, and repair modern electronics-dependent machinery, on the same favorable terms given to authorized dealers. It would let people bypass software locks for repair purposes, void the manufacturers' copyrights and patents if they stop supplying required items, and put the Federal Trade Commission in charge of enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers and ranchers who own or lease modern equipment, and independent repair shops. A tractor today can depend on embedded software for basic functions, and manufacturers generally restrict access to the diagnostic tools, software, parts, and manuals needed to fix them, which pushes owners toward dealer service at dealer prices and can leave a machine idle during planting or harvest while waiting for an authorized technician. The bill would force manufacturers to sell those repair inputs at no more than their best dealer price, make repair documentation free, bar software "pairing locks" that block aftermarket parts, and let owners legally bypass copyright-based software restrictions for repair. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to offer any owner or independent shop the documentation, parts, software, and tools needed to diagnose, maintain, or repair electronics-enabled farm equipment, on the same terms and at the same lowest price offered to authorized dealers.

Makes repair documentation available free of charge and repair software tools free, offline-capable, and unconditionally usable, so a farmer is not locked out of fixing a machine without an internet connection or manufacturer permission.
Bans requirements that parts be registered, paired, or approved by the manufacturer or a dealer before they will operate, the mechanism that can make an aftermarket or salvaged part useless.

Allows owners and independent shops to bypass copyright-protected software locks for diagnosis, maintenance, repair, interoperability, security research, or lawful modification, overriding the portion of copyright law that otherwise makes such circumvention illegal.
Creates a stiff consequence for noncompliance: if a manufacturer stops providing required repair materials, its copyrights and patents on those items fall into the public domain.
Requires that parts be replaceable without damaging the machine using commonly available tools or tools the manufacturer must sell on fair terms.
Puts the Federal Trade Commission in charge of enforcement, treating violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and requires the agency to write implementing rules.

analysis.who_pays: Agricultural equipment manufacturers and their dealer networks. They would lose some control over, and revenue from, repair service, diagnostic software, and proprietary parts, and would have to distribute documentation for free. If they stopped supplying required items, they would forfeit copyright and patent protection over those items. The bill's supporters generally argued that any equipment price increase would be small relative to repair savings; the record does not quantify it. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Farm equipment manufacturers and their dealers

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers have long argued that opening diagnostic software and emissions- and safety-related controls to third parties creates cybersecurity, safety, and equipment-tampering risks. The bill tries to address this: it preserves trade secrets except where needed for repair, and it does not allow deactivating safety notification systems, making permanent changes that violate safety or emissions laws, or evading emissions or copyright law. Critics could still argue those lines are hard to police once circumvention tools circulate.

The penalty is unusually heavy and arguably poorly targeted: a single failure to supply one item would place that item's copyright and patent into the public domain, potentially surrendering valuable intellectual property over a repair document or component. An honest supporter would acknowledge this remedy goes far beyond typical FTC enforcement.

The bill covers only equipment 'exclusively used by the owner' in the owner's own agricultural operations, and leaves OEM-dealer agreements otherwise intact, so it would not reach every repair situation and would rely on FTC rulemaking to give the fair-and-reasonable terms practical meaning.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it covers, the benefits are concrete and immediate: lower repair bills, faster turnaround during time-critical seasons, and the ability to use independent shops or do the work themselves. The costs fall on a small set of large manufacturers, mostly as lost repair revenue and compliance burden. The real weaknesses are in the design: the public-domain forfeiture penalty is a blunt instrument, and the safety and cybersecurity concerns the industry raises are addressed by carve-outs rather than a tested regime. On balance this is a consumer- and farmer-protective bill whose main cost is a transfer of power (and some revenue) away from a concentrated equipment-manufacturing industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Tester introduced the Agricultural Right to Repair Act on February 1, 2022, joined by Sen. Ben Ray Lujan as the bill's only cosponsor.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
That was the last action of any kind: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll-call vote ever occurred before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Because a bill must pass both chambers and be signed to become law, the bill's complete lack of committee action ended it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agricultural equipment manufacturers, whose repair and parts business was protected simply by the bill never moving. Farmers gained nothing; the repair restrictions the bill targeted remain unchanged by federal law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm equipment makers kept the repair monopoly

for.name: Sen. Jon Tester
for.role: U.S. Senator from Montana; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Agricultural Right to Repair Act on February 1, 2022.

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Lujan
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Mexico; only cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other senators joined.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 1, 2022 and took no further action: no hearing, no markup, no vote. The chair never scheduled the bill.

against.name: Agricultural equipment manufacturers (e.g., John Deere) and dealer networks
against.role: Industry whose repair and parts business the bill targeted
against.what_they_did: The record contains no direct congressional action by the industry on this bill; equipment makers were publicly opposing right-to-repair requirements during this period, favoring voluntary commitments instead.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no partisan split can be measured; both the sponsor (Tester) and the sole cosponsor (Lujan) were Democrats, and the Democratic-run Commerce Committee never acted.

industries.industry: Agricultural equipment manufacturers (e.g., John Deere, CNH)
industries.note: The bill strips manufacturers of the power to restrict who can repair their machines and what parts can be used, and of the revenue that comes from routing repairs through authorized dealers at dealer-set prices. Its profit model depends on charging farmers for proprietary parts, software, and service, which is exactly what the bill requires them to share at cost.

industries.industry: Equipment dealers and authorized repair networks
industries.note: Dealers' service departments would face competition from owners and independent shops for the first time on equal terms, since the bill pegs what manufacturers may charge outsiders to their best dealer terms and voids dealer-agreement clauses that would block it.
Independent shops would gain legal access to manuals, diagnostic software, parts, and unlocking tools, letting them compete for repair work they are currently often locked out of.
